non-expert panelists have heterogeneous backgrounds and may not be optimized for independence.","Ensemble ML often uses weighted voting or stacking to optimize the aggregation; a non-expert panel typically uses simple averaging or majority vote, which may be suboptimal if panelists have heterogeneous competence.","The checklist in the panel acts as a constraint on the hypothesis space, whereas in standard bagging, the base classifiers see bootstrap samples of the data but are not constrained in the features they can use."],"overturn_conditions":["Empirical studies show that for the specific task domain, single experts have lower error rates than aggregated non-expert panels, indicating that tacit knowledge outweighs noise reduction.","It is demonstrated that the non-experts' judgments are highly correlated (rho > 0.8), meaning the panel provides no more information than a single non-expert.","The task is shown to be 'zero-noise' but 'high-complexity,' such that the variance-reduction benefit is irrelevant and the bias of the non-experts dominates."],"shared_structure":["A set of individually weak, high-variance estimators (non-experts/base classifiers) is combined via a simple aggregation rule (averaging/voting) to produce an estimator with lower variance than a single strong estimator (expert/complex model).","The success of the aggregation depends on the independence of the estimators and the validity of the features they use (the checklist).","For objectively verifiable outcomes, reliability is determined by the distance from the true outcome, which is a function of both bias and variance."],"source_memory_refs":["SRC_005","SRC_003","SRC_001"],"transfer_claims":["Just as a random forest outperforms a single deep tree by averaging away predictive of the outcome, no amount of aggregation will yield a reliable predictor."]},"claim":"Trained non-expert panels using explicit checklists will, on average, produce more reliable judgments and instead uses a consensus rule that amplifies shared biases.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"A single expert's intuition is a high-variance estimator: it depends on recent cases, mood, and salience biases. An explicit checklist forces every observer to sample the same diagnostic dimensions, converting what would be tacit, inconsistent weighting into a fixed, uniform measurement protocol. The panel then aggregates multiple independent draws from this standardized protocol. By the logic of the wisdom of the crowd and the bias-variance tradeoff, averaging multiple non-expert judgments reduces non-systematic error (noise) faster than it accumulates systematic error (bias), provided the checklist is valid. For verifiable outcomes, reliability is precisely a function of variance, so the panel's averaged estimate should be closer to the true outcome more often than a single expert's un-averaged intuition.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
